title: Harun al-Rashid and the Arab Girl (తెలుగు)

full_text:
The Caliph Harun al-Rashid was hunting across the desert of the Hijaz with his vizier Ja'afar and a retinue of guards. Becoming separated from his companions in pursuit of an antelope, the Caliph stopped near an isolated spring where a young Bedouin maiden of the Banu Kilab was watering her camel.

The Caliph, dressed in simple hunting garments, called out: 'Peace be upon you, maiden! Draw water for a thirsty traveler.'

The girl handed him a clean wooden bowl of cold spring water with graceful courtesy. As he drank, the Caliph noticed her dignified bearing, clear eyes, and asked: 'Who are you, and what is your clan?'

The maiden answered in spontaneous, rhyming verse:
'I am a maiden of the desert sands,
Where freedom dwells and honor commands;
Our hearths are open to the traveler’s need,
And valor guides every word and deed!'

Harun al-Rashid, delighted by her poetic fluency, resolved to test her wit. He recited an intricate riddle of grammar and ancient lineage; she answered on the spot with flawless meter, quoting the pre-Islamic poets with effortless mastery.

At that moment, Ja'afar and twenty royal horsemen galloped up, dismounting and bowing to the dust: 'Peace be upon you, O Commander of the Faithful!'

The maiden did not tremble or lose her composure before the Emperor of the East. She stepped forward, bowed with royal dignity, and said: 'If you are indeed the shepherd of the nations, O Caliph, remember that the desert child who gave you water was proud to quench the thirst of an honest man!'

Enchanted by her peerless wit, courage, and virtue, Harun al-Rashid rewarded her tribe with a thousand sheep, granted her father a pension, and celebrated her as the jewel of the desert.
moral: Natural intelligence, spontaneous wit, and dignity are born in desert freedom, rivaling imperial courts. [TE]
